summary: Earth Jukebox turns NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into live music. The browser reads each video frame (brightness, colour, motion, sudden flashes) and generates sound from it in real time, so a lightning flash on the left of the map is a drum hit in your left ear. It addresses the challenge by making visual Earth science usable without sight: you can also explore any frame by touch or keyboard and hear what is under your finger.
details:
What it does: Pick a NASA visualization like a record and hear it. Ten records cover lightning, night lights, ocean currents, aerosols, CO2, air quality, forests, an atmospheric river, and a live "Earth Today" image. Earth Band plays several visualizations together as one band.

How it works: Each video frame is drawn to a small grid in the browser and analysed about 15 times a second. A separate music clock reads those features on every beat and plays synthesized instruments. One sound language is used everywhere: instrument = what it is, left/right = position, pitch = height on the map, loudness = how much. Every note draws a ripple at its source.

Benefits: Earth science becomes usable without sight. Full keyboard control, explore-by-touch that works while playing or paused, captions, a "learn the sounds" legend, and reduced-motion support. We ran listening, visual and NVDA screen-reader checks with 15 participants.

Limits: this is a sonification of the rendered visualizations, not the raw data, and it is not an official NASA product.

Next: sound from the underlying data, more languages, and co-design with blind and low-vision listeners.

Tools: JavaScript, Vite, Tone.js, Canvas 2D, Web Workers, ffmpeg. Built with help from an AI assistant (Claude) for planning, code and documentation.
